  L44: This wrapper dispatches every blocking SQLite operation to a thread pool via ``loop.run_in_executor()`` because

  L48: :param lock_file: path to the SQLite database file used as the lock
  L54: single-thread executor so every operation runs on the same thread (SQLite affinity requires this) and shuts it

===== backend_ai\venv311\Lib\site-packages\sqlalchemy\dialects\sqlite\aiosqlite.py =====
  L1: # dialects/sqlite/aiosqlite.py
  L11: .. dialect:: sqlite+aiosqlite
  L12: :name: aiosqlite
  L13: :dbapi: aiosqlite
  L14: :connectstring: sqlite+aiosqlite:///file_path
  L15: :url: https://pypi.org/project/aiosqlite/
  L17: The aiosqlite dialect provides support for the SQLAlchemy asyncio interface
  L18: running on top of pysqlite.
  L20: aiosqlite is a wrapper around pysqlite that uses a background thread for
  L21: each connection.   It does not actually use non-blocking IO, as SQLite
  L25: Using a special asyncio mediation layer, the aiosqlite dialect is usable
  L34: engine = create_async_engine("sqlite+aiosqlite:///filename")
  L36: The URL passes through all arguments to the ``pysqlite`` driver, so all
  L37: connection arguments are the same as they are for that of :ref:`pysqlite`.
  L39: .. _aiosqlite_udfs:
  L44: aiosqlite extends pysqlite to support async, so we can create our own user-defined functions (UDFs)
  L45: in Python and use them directly in SQLite queries as described here: :ref:`pysqlite_udfs`.
  L47: .. _aiosqlite_serializable:
  L53: at the top level of the SQLAlchemy SQLite documentation, in the section
  L54: :ref:`sqlite_transactions`.
  L57: .. _aiosqlite_pooling:
  L62: The SQLAlchemy ``aiosqlite`` DBAPI establishes the connection pool differently
  L63: based on the kind of SQLite database that's requested:
